title: Middle of the Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the middle node of a singly linked list; for an even number of nodes, return the second middle.
Idea: Use `slow` and `fast` node references, advancing them by one and two links respectively; when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` points to the required middle.
Technique and why it applies: Fast and slow pointers locate the second middle in one pass without storing nodes.
Invariant: Each loop iteration advances `slow` half as many nodes as `fast`, so termination leaves `slow` at the second middle for even lengths.
Edge cases: An empty list returns null; a one-node list returns its head; an even-length list deliberately selects the later middle.
Complexity: Each node is traversed at most a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: Fast and slow pointers locate the second middle in one pass without storing nodes.

title: Middle of the Linked List
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the middle node of a singly linked list; for an even number of nodes, return the second middle.
Idea: Use `slow` and `fast` node references, advancing them by one and two links respectively; when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` points to the required middle.
Technique and why it applies: Fast and slow pointers locate the second middle in one pass without storing nodes.
Invariant: Each loop iteration advances `slow` half as many nodes as `fast`, so termination leaves `slow` at the second middle for even lengths.
Edge cases: An empty list returns null; a one-node list returns its head; an even-length list deliberately selects the later middle.
Complexity: Each node is traversed at most a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
code: class Solution { public ListNode middleNode(ListNode head){ListNode slow=head,fast=head;while(fast!=null&&fast.next!=null){slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next.next;}return slow;} }
complexity_reason: Fast and slow pointers locate the second middle in one pass without storing nodes.

title: Projection Area of 3D Shapes
approach_name: Sum top, row, and column projections
notes:
Task and constraints: For a grid of column heights, return the total area of its projections onto the xy, yz, and zx planes.
Idea: Count each positive grid cell for the top view, add each row maximum for the front view, and each column maximum for the side view.
Technique and why it applies: A positive cell contributes one top square, while row and column maxima give the two side projections.
Invariant: The three accumulators separately represent xy visible unit squares, row silhouettes, and column silhouettes; their sum is the total projection area.
Edge cases: Zero-height cells add no top-view square; empty grid returns zero; each row and column contributes only its maximum height.
Complexity: Every cell is inspected a constant number of times, giving O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: A positive cell contributes one top square, while row and column maxima give the two side projections.

title: Projection Area of 3D Shapes
approach_name: Sum top, row, and column projections
notes:
Task and constraints: For a grid of column heights, return the total area of its projections onto the xy, yz, and zx planes.
Idea: Count each positive grid cell for the top view, add each row maximum for the front view, and each column maximum for the side view.
Technique and why it applies: A positive cell contributes one top square, while row and column maxima give the two side projections.
Invariant: The three accumulators separately represent xy visible unit squares, row silhouettes, and column silhouettes; their sum is the total projection area.
Edge cases: Zero-height cells add no top-view square; empty grid returns zero; each row and column contributes only its maximum height.
Complexity: Every cell is inspected a constant number of times, giving O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int projectionArea(int[][] grid){if(grid.length==0)return 0;int top=0,rows=0,cols=0;for(int r=0;r<grid.length;r++){int max=0;for(int c=0;c<grid[0].length;c++){if(grid[r][c]>0)top++;max=Math.max(max,grid[r][c]);}rows+=max;}for(int c=0;c<grid[0].length;c++){int max=0;for(int r=0;r<grid.length;r++)max=Math.max(max,grid[r][c]);cols+=max;}return top+rows+cols;} }
complexity_reason: A positive cell contributes one top square, while row and column maxima give the two side projections.

title: Uncommon Words from Two Sentences
notes:
Task and constraints: Return words that occur exactly once across the two sentences.
Idea: Concatenate the sentences, split into words, count each word, and return entries whose total frequency is exactly one.
Technique and why it applies: Counting the combined token stream distinguishes words occurring once overall from words repeated across either sentence.
Invariant: The counter/map records occurrences across both sentences together, so a word repeated in either or both sentences is excluded.
Edge cases: A word appearing once is included; repeated words are omitted; output order is not specified by the problem.
Complexity: Counting and collecting words takes O(n) time and O(n) space for the frequency map.
complexity_reason: Counting the combined token stream distinguishes words occurring once overall from words repeated across either sentence.

title: Uncommon Words from Two Sentences
notes:
Task and constraints: Return words that occur exactly once across the two sentences.
Idea: Concatenate the sentences, split into words, count each word, and return entries whose total frequency is exactly one.
Technique and why it applies: Counting the combined token stream distinguishes words occurring once overall from words repeated across either sentence.
Invariant: The counter/map records occurrences across both sentences together, so a word repeated in either or both sentences is excluded.
Edge cases: A word appearing once is included; repeated words are omitted; output order is not specified by the problem.
Complexity: Counting and collecting words takes O(n) time and O(n) space for the frequency map.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public String[] uncommonFromSentences(String s1,String s2){Map<String,Integer>m=new HashMap<>();for(String w:(s1+" "+s2).split(" ")){m.put(w,m.getOrDefault(w,0)+1);}List<String>out=new ArrayList<>();for(String w:m.keySet())if(m.get(w)==1)out.add(w);return out.toArray(new String[0]);} }
complexity_reason: Counting the combined token stream distinguishes words occurring once overall from words repeated across either sentence.

title: Fair Candy Swap
notes:
Task and constraints: Return one candy-size pair to swap so Alice and Bob have equal total candy, assuming a solution exists.
Idea: Let `delta=(sum(A)-sum(B))/2`; for each Alice size `x`, look for `x-delta` in a set of Bob's sizes.
Technique and why it applies: The half-difference equation reduces each candidate Alice candy to one required Bob size lookup.
Invariant: After swapping `x` for `y`, equal totals require `x-y` to equal half the difference between original sums.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees a solution; duplicate sizes do not affect set membership; the method returns the first valid pair found.
Complexity: Building the set and scanning both arrays takes O(n+m) time and O(m) extra space.
complexity_reason: The half-difference equation reduces each candidate Alice candy to one required Bob size lookup.

title: Fair Candy Swap
notes:
Task and constraints: Return one candy-size pair to swap so Alice and Bob have equal total candy, assuming a solution exists.
Idea: Let `delta=(sum(A)-sum(B))/2`; for each Alice size `x`, look for `x-delta` in a set of Bob's sizes.
Technique and why it applies: The half-difference equation reduces each candidate Alice candy to one required Bob size lookup.
Invariant: After swapping `x` for `y`, equal totals require `x-y` to equal half the difference between original sums.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees a solution; duplicate sizes do not affect set membership; the method returns the first valid pair found.
Complexity: Building the set and scanning both arrays takes O(n+m) time and O(m) extra space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int[] fairCandySwap(int[] a,int[] b){int delta=(Arrays.stream(a).sum()-Arrays.stream(b).sum())/2;Set<Integer>s=new HashSet<>();for(int x:b)s.add(x);for(int x:a)if(s.contains(x-delta))return new int[]{x,x-delta};return new int[0];} }
complexity_reason: The half-difference equation reduces each candidate Alice candy to one required Bob size lookup.

title: Monotonic Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if an array is entirely nondecreasing or entirely nonincreasing.
Idea: Check whether every adjacent pair is nondecreasing or every adjacent pair is nonincreasing.
Technique and why it applies: Testing both adjacent-order predicates captures either permitted monotonic direction, including constant arrays.
Invariant: Each comparison rules out a direction only when it finds a violating adjacent pair; the array qualifies if either direction survives.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values are allowed; empty and single-element arrays satisfy both directional checks.
Complexity: The two linear checks take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
class Solution:
 def isMonotonic(self,nums):return all(nums[i]<=nums[i+1] for i in range(len(nums)-1)) or all(nums[i]>=nums[i+1] for i in range(len(nums)-1))
complexity_reason: Testing both adjacent-order predicates captures either permitted monotonic direction, including constant arrays.

title: Monotonic Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if an array is entirely nondecreasing or entirely nonincreasing.
Idea: Check whether every adjacent pair is nondecreasing or every adjacent pair is nonincreasing.
Technique and why it applies: Testing both adjacent-order predicates captures either permitted monotonic direction, including constant arrays.
Invariant: Each comparison rules out a direction only when it finds a violating adjacent pair; the array qualifies if either direction survives.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values are allowed; empty and single-element arrays satisfy both directional checks.
Complexity: The two linear checks take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public boolean isMonotonic(int[] a){boolean inc=true,dec=true;for(int i=1;i<a.length;i++){if(a[i]<a[i-1])inc=false;if(a[i]>a[i-1])dec=false;}return inc||dec;} }
complexity_reason: Testing both adjacent-order predicates captures either permitted monotonic direction, including constant arrays.

title: Increasing Order Search Tree
approach_name: Inorder rebuild as a right-only chain
notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange a BST so its inorder sequence becomes a tree with no left children and only right children.
Idea: Traverse the BST inorder; the Python version relinks each visited node through a `tail`, while the Java version stores inorder values and builds a right-only chain.
Technique and why it applies: Inorder order is sorted for a BST, so linking visited values sequentially creates the required increasing chain.
Invariant: Inorder traversal visits BST values in sorted order, and each emitted node is linked after the previous one with no left child.
Edge cases: A null tree yields null; the output contains every original value in sorted order; recursion depth depends on tree height.
Complexity: Traversal and reconstruction take O(n) time; auxiliary space is O(h) recursion for the relinking version and O(n) values/nodes for the rebuilding version.
complexity_reason: Inorder order is sorted for a BST, so linking visited values sequentially creates the required increasing chain.

title: Increasing Order Search Tree
approach_name: Inorder rebuild as a right-only chain
notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange a BST so its inorder sequence becomes a tree with no left children and only right children.
Idea: Traverse the BST inorder; the Python version relinks each visited node through a `tail`, while the Java version stores inorder values and builds a right-only chain.
Technique and why it applies: Inorder order is sorted for a BST, so linking visited values sequentially creates the required increasing chain.
Invariant: Inorder traversal visits BST values in sorted order, and each emitted node is linked after the previous one with no left child.
Edge cases: A null tree yields null; the output contains every original value in sorted order; recursion depth depends on tree height.
Complexity: Traversal and reconstruction take O(n) time; auxiliary space is O(h) recursion for the relinking version and O(n) values/nodes for the rebuilding version.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public TreeNode increasingBST(TreeNode root){List<Integer>v=new ArrayList<>();inorder(root,v);TreeNode dummy=new TreeNode(0),cur=dummy;for(int x:v){cur.right=new TreeNode(x);cur=cur.right;}return dummy.right;}private void inorder(TreeNode n,List<Integer>v){if(n!=null){inorder(n.left,v);v.add(n.val);inorder(n.right,v);}} }
complexity_reason: Inorder order is sorted for a BST, so linking visited values sequentially creates the required increasing chain.

title: Sort Array By Parity
notes:
Task and constraints: Return an array with all even integers before all odd integers.
Idea: Collect all even values before all odd values; the implementations preserve relative order within each partition by scanning the input in order.
Technique and why it applies: Separate stable passes partition values by parity without needing a comparison sort.
Invariant: After the even pass, the output prefix contains every even input value; the following pass appends all odd values.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return empty arrays; negative even values still satisfy remainder zero; relative order is not required but is preserved here.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and the returned array/list uses O(n) space.
code:
class Solution:
 def sortArrayByParity(self,nums):return [x for x in nums if x%2==0]+[x for x in nums if x%2!=0]
complexity_reason: Separate stable passes partition values by parity without needing a comparison sort.

title: Sort Array By Parity
notes:
Task and constraints: Return an array with all even integers before all odd integers.
Idea: Collect all even values before all odd values; the implementations preserve relative order within each partition by scanning the input in order.
Technique and why it applies: Separate stable passes partition values by parity without needing a comparison sort.
Invariant: After the even pass, the output prefix contains every even input value; the following pass appends all odd values.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return empty arrays; negative even values still satisfy remainder zero; relative order is not required but is preserved here.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and the returned array/list uses O(n) space.
code: class Solution { public int[] sortArrayByParity(int[] nums){int[]a=new int[nums.length];int i=0;for(int x:nums)if(x%2==0)a[i++]=x;for(int x:nums)if(x%2!=0)a[i++]=x;return a;} }
complexity_reason: Separate stable passes partition values by parity without needing a comparison sort.

title: Smallest Range I
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest possible difference between maximum and minimum after each value may change by at most k.
Idea: Find the original minimum and maximum and return `max(0, maximum-minimum-2*k)`.
Technique and why it applies: The range can shrink by at most k from each endpoint, so only the residual positive spread remains.
Invariant: Each endpoint can move inward by at most `k`, shrinking the range by at most `2*k`; a negative result is clamped to zero.
Edge cases: If the original spread is at most `2*k`, all values can be brought to a common value; input has at least one element.
Complexity: Finding extrema takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
class Solution:
 def smallestRangeI(self,nums,k):return max(0,max(nums)-min(nums)-2*k)
complexity_reason: The range can shrink by at most k from each endpoint, so only the residual positive spread remains.

title: Smallest Range I
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest possible difference between maximum and minimum after each value may change by at most k.
Idea: Find the original minimum and maximum and return `max(0, maximum-minimum-2*k)`.
Technique and why it applies: The range can shrink by at most k from each endpoint, so only the residual positive spread remains.
Invariant: Each endpoint can move inward by at most `k`, shrinking the range by at most `2*k`; a negative result is clamped to zero.
Edge cases: If the original spread is at most `2*k`, all values can be brought to a common value; input has at least one element.
Complexity: Finding extrema takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int smallestRangeI(int[] nums,int k){int min=Integer.MAX_VALUE,max=Integer.MIN_VALUE;for(int x:nums){min=Math.min(min,x);max=Math.max(max,x);}return Math.max(0,max-min-2*k);} }
complexity_reason: The range can shrink by at most k from each endpoint, so only the residual positive spread remains.

title: X of a Kind in a Deck of Cards
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the deck can be split into groups of equal size X, where X is at least 2 and every group contains identical cards.
Idea: Count each card value and compute the greatest common divisor of all positive frequencies; a common group size of at least two exists exactly when that GCD is at least two.
Technique and why it applies: A group size divides every frequency, and the GCD gives the largest common divisor that can be at least two.
Invariant: The GCD divides every card count, so it is the largest group size that can partition every value into equal identical-card groups.
Edge cases: A deck with any frequency equal to one forces the GCD to one; the Java count array relies on the bounded card-value domain.
Complexity: Counting and reducing frequencies takes O(n) time; auxiliary storage is O(1) under the bounded value domain (or O(u) for u distinct values).
code:
from collections import Counter
from math import gcd
from functools import reduce
class Solution:
 def hasGroupsSizeX(self,deck):return reduce(gcd,Counter(deck).values())>=2
complexity_reason: A group size divides every frequency, and the GCD gives the largest common divisor that can be at least two.

title: X of a Kind in a Deck of Cards
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the deck can be split into groups of equal size X, where X is at least 2 and every group contains identical cards.
Idea: Count each card value and compute the greatest common divisor of all positive frequencies; a common group size of at least two exists exactly when that GCD is at least two.
Technique and why it applies: A group size divides every frequency, and the GCD gives the largest common divisor that can be at least two.
Invariant: The GCD divides every card count, so it is the largest group size that can partition every value into equal identical-card groups.
Edge cases: A deck with any frequency equal to one forces the GCD to one; the Java count array relies on the bounded card-value domain.
Complexity: Counting and reducing frequencies takes O(n) time; auxiliary storage is O(1) under the bounded value domain (or O(u) for u distinct values).
code: class Solution { public boolean hasGroupsSizeX(int[] deck){int[]cnt=new int[10000];for(int x:deck)cnt[x]++;int g=0;for(int c:cnt)if(c>0)g=gcd(g,c);return g>=2;}private int gcd(int a,int b){while(b!=0){int t=a%b;a=b;b=t;}return a;} }
complexity_reason: A group size divides every frequency, and the GCD gives the largest common divisor that can be at least two.

title: Reverse Only Letters
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse only the letters in a string, leaving non-letter characters in their original positions.
Idea: Use left and right pointers, skipping nonletters and swapping only when both pointers identify letters.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers exchange only letter positions, leaving all non-letter positions untouched.
Invariant: The letter sequence becomes reversed while every nonletter remains at its original index because the pointers pass over symbols without moving them.
Edge cases: Strings with no letters remain unchanged; punctuation and digits stay fixed; empty and one-character strings need no swaps.
Complexity: The pointers scan the string once for O(n) time, and a character array/list requires O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Two pointers exchange only letter positions, leaving all non-letter positions untouched.

title: Reverse Only Letters
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse only the letters in a string, leaving non-letter characters in their original positions.
Idea: Use left and right pointers, skipping nonletters and swapping only when both pointers identify letters.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers exchange only letter positions, leaving all non-letter positions untouched.
Invariant: The letter sequence becomes reversed while every nonletter remains at its original index because the pointers pass over symbols without moving them.
Edge cases: Strings with no letters remain unchanged; punctuation and digits stay fixed; empty and one-character strings need no swaps.
Complexity: The pointers scan the string once for O(n) time, and a character array/list requires O(n) space.
code: class Solution { public String reverseOnlyLetters(String s){char[]a=s.toCharArray();int l=0,r=a.length-1;while(l<r){if(!Character.isLetter(a[l]))l++;else if(!Character.isLetter(a[r]))r--;else{char t=a[l];a[l]=a[r];a[r]=t;l++;r--;}}return new String(a);} }
complexity_reason: Two pointers exchange only letter positions, leaving all non-letter positions untouched.
